attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, not a quotation of others.

semantics.note: The claim is a firm general statement that near-perfect but imperfect automation makes human inattention more likely. The proposition and its imperfect-system qualifier match the text.

contract.note: Reading the claim as a general tendency, measured by both monitoring performance and mind wandering, is an ordinary plain reading. Splitting 'space out' into those two measures shapes the result and points to a mixed outcome.

evidence.note: Peer-reviewed 2018 study (abstract only): monitoring was poorer with 90% reliable automation than with 50%. It compares just two levels and does not test the near-perfect range.

Peer-reviewed 2018 study with 16 participants: mind wandering did not change with automation reliability, though trust and mental demand did. This is a null result on the subjective attention measure.

reviews.rationale: Under the contract's measures, the monitoring-performance part holds: e1 found poorer monitoring with more reliable automation. The mind-wandering part does not: e2 found mind wandering unchanged across reliability levels. Neither study tests the gradient close to perfection. The contract allows a mixed result when findings differ across attention measures.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps both the 41-of-77 count and the claim that the errors were missed because editors were inattentive. It drops 'subtle but important', which is a small loss.

contract.note: Reading 'last week' as the week the errors were found and corrected is fair. Requiring direct evidence of inattention, rather than treating missed errors as proof of it, is a strict but defensible reading of the cause Marcus asserted.

evidence.note: Contemporaneous Verge report dated Jan 25, 2023: CNET issued corrections on 41 of the 77 AI-written stories. This matches the count.
CNET's own disclosure: editors outlined, expanded and edited the AI drafts. Some corrections were for minor issues or wording that was not original. Nothing here shows the editors were inattentive.

reviews.rationale: The count holds: e1 confirms corrections on 41 of the 77 AI-assisted articles. The explanation is not established: the packet has no direct evidence that inattentive editors caused the missed errors. CNET also says some corrections were minor or about originality rather than important factual errors.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: The sentence 'and so they editors trusted them' is a firm causal claim. The earlier counterfactual uses 'might', and the nearby 'probably' sentence is separate, so neither hedge governs this assertion.

contract.note: Asking for evidence that polished prose led to misplaced editorial trust fits the mechanism Marcus asserted.

evidence.note: CNET's own account of active editing. It neither confirms nor rules out editors over-trusting the drafts.
Verge report of corrections on 41 of 77 stories. It establishes that errors were published, not why editors missed them.

reviews.rationale: The evidence shows that erroneous content was published, but nothing in the packet links the articles' polished surface to editors trusting them. No editorial record or testimony establishes or rules out that mechanism.

attribution.note: Marcus's own prediction in his post.

semantics.note: 'Going to happen a whole lot more this year' is unhedged, so it is a scored forecast with a 2023 horizon. The hedged 'likely' is in the following sentence and does not apply here.

contract.note: Reading the claim as a substantial increase in 2023, compared with before the post, is a fair plain reading. Marcus named no baseline or counting unit, so the result depends on how incidents are counted.

evidence.note: Feb 2023 Futurism report of an error-filled AI-assisted health article at Men's Journal. It shows the problem recurred after the post, but not that it became more frequent.
Irish Times editor's note, May 2023, on a hoax column that may have been AI-made. This was deliberate deception, not editors over-trusting AI output.
July 2023 Gizmodo case: an erroneous AI article was published while the section editors were bypassed. The mechanism differs from editorial over-trust.
NewsGuard tracked unreliable AI news sites rising from 49 in May to over 600 in December 2023. These are site counts with no human oversight, not erroneous articles that editors accepted.

reviews.rationale: The 2023 horizon has passed. The packet shows that individual incidents happened and that AI content farms grew, but it has no comparable before-and-after count of erroneous AI articles getting past editorial scrutiny. It therefore cannot establish or refute a substantial increase.
